This vignette demonstrates our homemade `ridgereg()` function for ridge regression.

Ordinary least‑squares regression can produce unstable coefficient estimates in the presence of multicollinearity.
Ridge regression introduces an L2‑penalty term to shrink parameter estimates, controlled by the tuning parameter $\lambda$.

The ridge estimator is given by

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{ridge} = (X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.$$

We will show coefficient paths, k‑fold cross‑validation for selecting optimal $\lambda$,
and compare ridge regression results with forward‑subset selection on the BostonHousing dataset.

We use the Boston housing dataset for our ridge regression demonstration. Our target variable is `medv`, the median house value.

```{r libraries}
library(mylinreg)   # our package: ridgereg() and linreg()
library(mlbench)    # BostonHousing data
library(caret)      # data splitting, train(), cross-validation
library(ggplot2)

data("BostonHousing")
```

The data set has `r nrow(BostonHousing)` observations of the median house value
`medv` and `r ncol(BostonHousing) - 1` covariates.

## Training and test data

```{r split}
train_idx <- createDataPartition(BostonHousing$medv, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_df <- BostonHousing[train_idx, ]
test_df <- BostonHousing[-train_idx, ]

ctrl_cv <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)
rmse <- function(obs, pred) sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2))

dim(train_df)
dim(test_df)
```

## Ordinary linear regression

```{r lm-model}
fit_lm <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl_cv)
fit_lm$results[, c("RMSE", "Rsquared")]

rmse_lm_train <- rmse(train_df$medv, predict(fit_lm, newdata = train_df))
rmse_lm_train
```

## Forward selection

Forward selection is a greedy subset‑selection approach.
It starts with empty model and iteratively adds one predictor that gives the largest improvement in model performance, until no further improvement can be made.
We compare the prediction performance from forward‑selected subset versus full‑model ridge regression.

`method = "leapForward"` uses the `leaps` package. The grid `nvmax = 1:p`
covers models with 1 up to all `r ncol(train_df) - 1` covariates, and the
intercept-only model (0 covariates) is fitted separately, so models with
0, 1, ..., p covariates are all compared.

```{r forward}
fit_forward <- train(
  medv ~ .,
  data = train_df,
  method = "leapForward",
  trControl = ctrl_cv,
  tuneGrid = data.frame(nvmax = 1:(ncol(train_df) - 1))
)

fit_forward$bestTune
head(fit_forward$results[order(fit_forward$results$RMSE),
                         c("nvmax", "RMSE")])

## Intercept-only model, for the comparison with 0 covariates.
null_fit <- lm(medv ~ 1, data = train_df)

data.frame(
  model = c("intercept only", "OLS (all covariates)", "forward selection"),
  covariates = c(0, ncol(train_df) - 1, fit_forward$bestTune$nvmax),
  train_RMSE = round(c(
    rmse(train_df$medv, predict(null_fit, newdata = train_df)),
    rmse_lm_train,
    rmse(train_df$medv, predict(fit_forward, newdata = train_df))
  ), 3)
)
```

## A custom caret model for ridgereg()

`caret::train()` accepts a custom model: `fit()` estimates the model for one
value of the tuning parameter and `predict()` scores new data.

```{r custom-model}
ridgereg_caret <- list(
  label = "Ridge regression (mylinreg)",
  library = "mylinreg",
  type = "Regression",
  parameters = data.frame(parameter = "lambda",
                          class = "numeric", label = "lambda"),
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-2, 3, length.out = len))
  },
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
    ridgereg(y ~ ., data = data.frame(y = y, x), lambda = param$lambda)
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
    as.numeric(predict(modelFit, newdata = newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  sort = function(x) x[order(x$lambda), ]
)
```

## Ridge regression for different values of lambda

First we fit a ridge regression with a manually chosen penalty λ = 1 and inspect coefficient estimates.
When λ = 0, ridge regression reduces to ordinary least squares regression.

```{r ridge-lambdas}
lambdas <- c(0, 1, 10, 100)

data.frame(
  lambda = lambdas,
  train_RMSE = round(vapply(lambdas, function(l) {
    fit <- ridgereg(medv ~ ., data = train_df, lambda = l)
    rmse(train_df$medv, predict(fit, newdata = train_df))
  }, numeric(1)), 3)
)
```

## Tuning lambda with 10-fold cross-validation

The choice of λ is critical. We use k‑fold cross‑validation to find the optimal penalty that minimises test‑set mean squared error.

```{r cv-ridge}
fit_ridge <- train(
  medv ~ .,
  data = train_df,
  method = ridgereg_caret,
  trControl = ctrl_cv,
  tuneGrid = data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-2, 3, length.out = 12))
)

best_lambda <- fit_ridge$bestTune$lambda
fit_ridge$results[, c("lambda", "RMSE")]
best_lambda
```

```{r cv-plot}
ggplot(fit_ridge$results, aes(x = lambda, y = RMSE)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_lambda, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "10-fold cross-validated RMSE",
       x = expression(lambda), y = "RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The cross-validation selects `lambda =` `r signif(best_lambda, 3)`.

## Evaluation on the test data

```{r test}
pred_lm <- predict(fit_lm, newdata = test_df)
pred_forward <- predict(fit_forward, newdata = test_df)
pred_ridge <- predict(fit_ridge, newdata = test_df)

data.frame(
  model = c("OLS (all covariates)", "forward selection",
            paste0("ridge (lambda = ", signif(best_lambda, 3), ")")),
  test_RMSE = round(c(rmse(test_df$medv, pred_lm),
                      rmse(test_df$medv, pred_forward),
                      rmse(test_df$medv, pred_ridge)), 3)
)
```

## Conclusion

The three models have a similar test RMSE
(`r round(rmse(test_df$medv, pred_lm), 3)` for OLS,
`r round(rmse(test_df$medv, pred_forward), 3)` for forward selection and
`r round(rmse(test_df$medv, pred_ridge), 3)` for ridge). This is expected:
`BostonHousing` has only `r ncol(train_df) - 1` covariates and little
collinearity, so there is not much variance for the penalty to remove.

What ridge regression does show is the shrinkage:

```{r shrinkage}
norm <- function(lambda) {
  sum(coef(ridgereg(medv ~ ., data = train_df, lambda = lambda))[-1]^2)
}
round(c(lambda0 = norm(0), best = norm(best_lambda)), 3)
```

The L2 norm of the coefficients falls from
`r round(norm(0), 1)` at `lambda = 0` to `r round(norm(best_lambda), 1)` at the
tuned penalty. Ridge regression pays off when covariates are many and
correlated, or when `p > n`: there the OLS solution is unstable (or does not
exist), while `ridgereg()` still returns finite, shrunken coefficients.
